title: Sony's ECM-AX10: A ¥27,000 Compact Mic That Records Spatial Audio Straight Into Your Smartphone
summary: Sony launches ECM-AX10 compact microphone for spatial audio recording on smartphones
detailed: Sony's plug-in microphone, the ECM-AX10, is gaining traction as an easy entry point into spatial audio recording.

Users can choose from four export formats: MP4 with Eclipsa Audio, MP4 with binaural audio that reproduces spatial breadth through two left and right channels, MP4 with ordinary stereo audio, and WAV containing only the Ambisonics audio.

Eclipsa Audio is a spatial audio technology developed chiefly by Google and Samsung, based on the "Immersive Audio Model and Formats (IAMF)" specification from the Alliance for Open Media (AOMedia), the group behind the AV1 video codec.
In terms of market impact, the ECM-AX10 has the potential to broaden the base of spatial audio production.
sentences: Sony's plug-in microphone, the ECM-AX10, is gaining traction as an easy entry point into spatial audio recording.
The compact unit weighs just 24 grams and, simply by connecting directly to a smartphone, can capture sound in three dimensions — front, back, left, right, and up and down.

It is sold at an open price, but as of this writing its street price on Amazon.co.jp is around ¥27,000 (approximately $170) including tax, placing it in the low-price tier for spatial audio microphones.
The ECM-AX10's standout feature is its support for "Ambisonics recording," achieved by arranging four omnidirectional microphone units in a spherical layout.
Whereas ordinary stereo audio records sound in two left and right channels, first-order Ambisonics combines four components: W, X, Y, and Z.
W captures sound arriving from all directions combined; X represents front-back differences, Y left-right differences, and Z up-down differences.
By synthesizing these, the system records three-dimensional information including the direction from which sound arrives.

Sony says it has optimized the advanced signal processing used in higher-order Ambisonics microphones for four-channel first-order recording, and claims to achieve both ideal directivity across a wide band and balanced frequency characteristics from low to high frequencies.
Recorded audio is converted into spatial audio formats using the dedicated free app "Spatial Audio Video Tool," available for iOS and Android.
The app displays gain meters for all four channels, and its simple interface requires only pressing the record button.

Users can choose from four export formats: MP4 with Eclipsa Audio, MP4 with binaural audio that reproduces spatial breadth through two left and right channels, MP4 with ordinary stereo audio, and WAV containing only the Ambisonics audio.

Eclipsa Audio is a spatial audio technology developed chiefly by Google and Samsung, based on the "Immersive Audio Model and Formats (IAMF)" specification from the Alliance for Open Media (AOMedia), the group behind the AV1 video codec.
Unlike Dolby Atmos and similar formats, it is royalty-free — an advantage cited for its adoption.
YouTube already supports Eclipsa Audio, and playback on compatible devices lets viewers enjoy immersive sound.
Note: Specifications are as of the time of writing; video resolution is slated to support 4K in a future update.
Playback and editing environments, however, remain constrained.
Playing back the full four channels as recorded requires compatible hardware, which as of this writing is limited to certain Samsung and LG TVs and soundbars.
Headphones equipped with a compatible binaural renderer will play the audio as optimized spatial sound.
On the editing side, editing and exporting video while keeping the Eclipsa Audio (IAMF) format requires Adobe Premiere.

In other environments, users have no choice but to edit audio and video separately and then combine them with FFmpeg — a point cited as a challenge, since although recording itself is easy, the editing barrier is high.
Adding video editing features to the dedicated app would greatly improve convenience.
Cooperation with third-party apps is also limited.
When connected to Blackmagic Camera, which allows selection of audio input sources, the ECM-AX10 was recognized, but only two of its four channels were actually captured.
DaVinci Resolve Studio also does not support exporting in the Eclipsa Audio (IAMF) format, and a future update is awaited.
In terms of market impact, the ECM-AX10 has the potential to broaden the base of spatial audio production.

Previously, three-dimensional audio recording was a field requiring dedicated equipment and expertise, but a setup that is complete with a direct smartphone connection and a free app dramatically lowers the barrier to entry for uses such as video streaming, vlogs, and interview recording.
If the royalty-free Eclipsa Audio and YouTube's support reinforce each other, creators' options should expand as compatible devices proliferate.
That said, with playback-compatible devices currently limited to certain TVs and soundbars, the reach of produced spatial audio to viewers remains limited.
Whether editing workflows are improved and playback environments become more widespread is likely to determine the takeoff of the spatial audio market.
